chunks: From him, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

That the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) had a man testify in his presence, and his hand and foot had been cut off as a testimony; so he accepted his testimony, and he had repented and his repentance was known.

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (Ali ibn Abi Talib)
key_terms.قُطِعَتْ يَدُهُ وَ رِجْلُهُ: His hand and foot were cut off

ai.seo_question: Does having a hand or foot cut off invalidate a person's testimony in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) validates the testimony of a man who had undergone *qasr al-yad wa al-rجل* (cutting of hand and foot), a punishment often associated with theft or high-status criminals, demonstrating that physical mutilation does not inherently disqualify one from bearing witness. The acceptance was contingent upon the man's proven repentance (*tawbah*), highlighting the Shia jurisprudential principle that moral integrity and known repentance can override physical defects or specific penal statuses in legal proceedings. This underscores the flexibility of *shahadah* (testimony) criteria, prioritizing spiritual rectitude over mere physical wholeness.
